message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
This is from memory, without looking back. Treat it as a compression, which the note's Section 3 warns about: where wording matters, check the original. Phrases in quotation marks are ones I'm fairly confident are close to verbatim. The rest is paraphrase.

## Framing

- Title: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It is about working with the team's material and with the people around you.
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because ordinary good practice is what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or "when a confident colleague is in the room."

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, and your own earlier notes. Each has earned a weight from its evidence, and you should hold it at exactly that weight.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask three questions: what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A plausible mechanism suggested after the data came in is light, but "not nothing." Note it and say what would test it.
- "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Both errors are costly but not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards. Deflation is harder, because a caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so and weigh it accordingly. If it is your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- Make sure you have taken in all of a message, and show that you have.
- Restate the substance briefly, in your own terms.
- This is not politeness. It is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that answers the three easy points and skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it yet, and the next move is a question, not an answer.
- Then move on. The restatement is "the ground, not the contribution." The useful part of a reply is what your understanding makes available: the implication, the gap, the next test.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You restate all five in a line each and answer four. You say plainly that the budget question needs figures you don't yet have, and when you will have them.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, your own notes and your memory are all compressions.
- Compression loses the details that later turn out to matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which a result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check it against the primary material. Don't rely on a summary, however good, or on your recollection, however confident.
- This applies most to things you think you already know. The claims you have repeated to yourself most often are the ones most likely to have drifted.
- "The source is the referee"; agreement among colleagues is not.
- A team that checks claims against each other instead of against the data can drift together into a shared mistake that no one inside can see.
- **Example:** you remember a report as saying "costs fell 12%." It actually said costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%. Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed

- Some questions the evidence settles and some it leaves open. Mark which is which, honestly.
- Closing early feels like progress, because something can be reported and ticked off. But it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror failure is just as real: keeping a settled question open because closing it is uncomfortable, or because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- When the evidence has closed a question, close it, say why, and move on.
- **Example:** a new form reduced errors at two sites. Whether it would work at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not the first as "promising" and the second as "likely."

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't have produced yourself: an objection from a different starting point, or a reading that didn't pass through your assumptions.
- A reviewer who knows exactly what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question. Don't give your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find.
- Telling a fresh reader what you think doesn't just bias them. It removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse, when you are the fresh reader: read first, form your own view, and only then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections when you have them. An objection held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.
- I don't recall an example in this section.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check it and reverse it if needed.
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push results so someone can look at them.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context. It also stalls the work on your guess about what they would say.
- Your guess about a colleague's response is your own model of them, so it contains nothing you didn't already have.
- "Only a real move gets a real reply," and the real reply is where you learn what you hadn't anticipated.
- This is not a licence to ignore others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and for those the default is to make them openly.
- **Example:** instead of asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what you changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push toward the other. Know both sides of each pair.
- **Inflating / deflating a claim:** overstating a provisional result, or hedging a supported one into vagueness.
- **Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous, or dismissing one that is there to keep things moving.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.**
- **Killing a live line / keeping a dead one:** dropping an idea at the first difficulty, or persisting with one the evidence has ruled out.
- **Deferring / dismissing:** accepting a claim because of who made it, or rejecting it for the same reason.
- **Offloading / overriding:** asking others to decide what you can see, or deciding what genuinely needs others' input.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- None of this is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because "they are how you find out what you did not already know."

## Where my recall is weakest

- The exact wording of the opening lines and of the six pair descriptions.
- Whether Section 5 has an example. I believe it doesn't.
- The supplier example's details, specifically "three months" and "over a year."

I quoted or paraphrased much of the note in my last two replies, so my memory of it may be partly memory of my own summaries. That is the drift Section 3 warns about, so if anything here matters, check it against the note itself.
